Sanity check: 37 million ft^3 (1.048e6 m^3) gives a mean density of ~316 kg/m^3, plausible for a steel-frame tower that is mostly air. Exterior: 200,000 ft^3 of Indiana limestone and granite, 10 million bricks, 730 tons of aluminium and stainless steel. Height 1,454 ft (443.2 m) to antenna tip. Lot 79,288 ft^2. Grip material: Indiana limestone facade (min 4,000 psi = 27.6 MPa compressive, mat_indiana_limestone) anchored to a steel frame. Structural note: grip stress at 1 g is ~3.2e11 Pa, about 10,000x limestone strength. The building sits on caisson foundations to bedrock and cannot be lifted without first being cut free. Projected area not quantified.","who_when":"ESB fact sheet (current); ENR archive"},{"key":"great_pyramid_mass","category":"object_mass","label":"Great Pyramid of Giza mass","value_si":6000000000,"low_si":5500000000,"high_si":7000000000,"unit_si":"kg","display":"~6 million tonnes (range ~5.5 to 7 Mt)","status":"estimate","sources":[{"url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza","title":"Wikipedia - Great Pyramid ('estimated 2.3 million large blocks, weighing 6 million tonnes'; 5.5 Mt limestone, 8,000 t granite, 500,000 t mortar; volume ~2.6 million m^3; base 230.3 m)"},{"url":"https://www.soest.hawaii.edu/martel/Courses/GG454/Lec_03_2018.pptx.pdf","title":"U. Hawaii GG454 rock-properties lecture (limestone dry density 2.67-2.72 g/cm^3)"}],"notes":"Method: there is no direct measurement. The literature figure is ~6 Mt (5.5 Mt limestone + 0.5 Mt mortar + 8,000 t granite). Low bound: limestone alone, 5.5 Mt. High bound (my calculation): the full ~2.6e6 m^3 envelope at 2.67 to 2.72 t/m^3 gives ~7.0 Mt if it were solid limestone. The real figure is lower because the envelope includes a natural bedrock hillock and voids. Block counts are disputed (2.3 to ~4 million). Base 230.3 m per side; height 146.6 m originally, 138.5 m now. Grip material: limestone blocks set with mortar (UCS 6 to 245 MPa, mat_limestone_generic). Structural note: grip stress at 1 g is ~5.9e12 Pa. The pyramid is a pile of separate blocks, so a grip pulls out one block and the rest stays.","who_when":"Literature estimates; accessed 2026-10"},{"key":"great_pyramid_projected_area","category":"object_area","label":"Great Pyramid projected area","value_si":34725,"low_si":16881,"high_si":53038,"unit_si":"m^2","display":"~16,900 (face-on) to 53,000 m^2 (top); orientation mean ~34,700 m^2","status":"estimate","sources":[{"url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza","title":"Wikipedia - base 230.3 m, original height 146.6 m"}],"notes":"Ideal square pyramid with the original height. Slant height 186.4 m; total surface 138,901 m^2. Orientation mean = S/4 (Cauchy, convex body) = 34,725 m^2. Face-on silhouette is 0.5 x 230.3 x 146.6 = 16,881 m^2; top-down 53,038 m^2.","who_when":"Derived"},{"key":"mount_everest_mass","category":"object_mass","label":"Mount Everest mass (definition-dependent estimate)","value_si":370000000000000,"low_si":160000000000000,"high_si":1400000000000000,"unit_si":"kg","display":"~4e14 kg (range ~1.6e14 to 1.4e15 kg depending on where the mountain 'ends')","status":"estimate","sources":[{"url":"https://thehimalayantimes.com/nepal/everest-2-0-worlds-tallest-peaks-revised-height-revealed-stands-at-8848-86m/","title":"Himalayan Times - joint China-Nepal height 8,848.86 m (Dec 2020)"},{"url":"https://all-geo.org/metageologist/2012/06/the-geology-of-mount-everest/","title":"Metageologist - The Geology of Mount Everest (Qomolangma Fm limestone summit; Yellow Band below)"},{"url":"https://www.soest.hawaii.edu/martel/Courses/GG454/Lec_03_2018.pptx.pdf","title":"U. Hawaii rock-properties lecture (densities, UCS)"},{"url":"https://mounteverest.info/?p=4587","title":"Popular page repeating ~357 trillion lb (1.62e14 kg), origin untraceable"}],"notes":"My own calculation. I found no peer-reviewed or survey-agency mass estimate. Method: a right circular cone, V = pi r^2 h / 3, at rock density 2,700 kg/m^3 (2,600 to 2,800 changes the result by about 4%). Summit 8,848.86 m. Definition A (central value): the mountain ends at ~5,200 m, roughly the elevation of the main base camps (not verified), so relief h = 3.65 km, and base radius r = 6 km gives V = 138 km^3 and M = 3.7e14 kg. Low (r = 4 km, same h) gives 61 km^3 and 1.65e14 kg, close to the widely repeated but unsourced 1.62e14 kg. High (base at ~4,000 m valley floors, h = 4.85 km, r = 10 km) gives 508 km^3 and 1.4e15 kg. Counting only the summit pyramid above ~7,000 m (h = 1.85 km, r = 2 km) gives just ~2e13 kg. Rock below the chosen base plane, including the crustal root, is excluded by definition. Geology: the summit is the Qomolangma Formation (Ordovician limestone) above the Yellow Band (marble/limestone, ~8,600 m), with schists and gneisses lower. UCS: limestone 6 to 245, marble 55 to 274, schist 25 to 62, gneiss 50 to 230 MPa. Structural note: grip stress at 1 g is ~3.6e17 Pa. 'Lifting' Everest means quarrying it free of the crust, so model it as excavation, not a grip.","who_when":"Height: China-Nepal joint survey, 8 Dec 2020; mass derived 2026-10"},{"key":"mount_everest_projected_area","category":"object_area","label":"Everest cone-model projected areas","value_si":21900000,"low_si":14600000,"high_si":113000000,"unit_si":"m^2","display":"side ~2.2e7 m^2; footprint ~1.1e8 m^2 (r = 6 km cone)","status":"estimate","sources":[{"url":"https://thehimalayantimes.com/nepal/everest-2-0-worlds-tallest-peaks-revised-height-revealed-stands-at-8848-86m/","title":"Summit height 8,848.86 m"}],"notes":"For the central cone (r = 6 km, h = 3.65 km): side silhouette r*h = 2.19e7 m^2; footprint pi r^2 = 1.13e8 m^2. The low value is the side silhouette for r = 4 km. Air drag is irrelevant at this scale compared with the mass.","who_when":"Derived"},{"key":"cumulus_cloud_water_mass","category":"object_mass","label":"Typical (1 km^3) cumulus cloud - liquid water only","value_si":500000,"unit_si":"kg","display":"~500,000 kg (~1.1 million lb) of droplets","status":"estimate","sources":[{"url":"https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/how-much-does-a-cloud-weigh","title":"USGS Water Science School - How much does a cloud weigh?"},{"url":"https://www.earthdate.org/episodes/puffy-clouds-weigh-in","title":"EarthDate - Puffy clouds weigh in (same 0.5 g/m^3 assumption)"}],"notes":"USGS illustration: 1 km^3 = 1e9 m^3 x ~0.5 g/m^3 liquid water content = 5e8 g = ~500,000 kg. This counts droplets only. The air in the same volume is roughly 1e9 kg at ~1 kg/m^3 (my rough figure, not sourced). Real liquid water content and size vary widely, and the range was not sourced. Grip material: none. A cloud is suspended droplets in air with no structural strength. A 'grab' would just push air and droplets aside. Model it as moving air, not a rigid body. Cross-section: cloud_cross_section_area.","who_when":"USGS Water Science School (current)"},{"key":"cloud_cross_section_area","category":"object_area","label":"1 km x 1 km cumulus cross-section","value_si":1000000,"unit_si":"m^2","display":"~1e6 m^2","status":"estimate","sources":[{"url":"https://www.usgs.gov/special-topics/water-science-school/science/how-much-does-a-cloud-weigh","title":"USGS 1 km cube cloud"}],"notes":"Follows from the USGS 1 km cube assumption.","who_when":"Derived"},{"key":"moon_mass","category":"object_mass","label":"Moon","value_si":7.346e+22,"unit_si":"kg","display":"7.346e22 kg","status":"verified","sources":[{"url":"https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html","title":"NASA NSSDCA Moon Fact Sheet (updated 11 Jan 2024)"}],"notes":"Volumetric mean radius 1,737.4 km; mean density 3,344 kg/m^3; GM 4,902.8 km^3/s^2 (listed as 0.00490 x 10^6 km^3/s^2); mean Earth-Moon distance 384,400 km. Not a 'grip' object. It is a self-gravitating body, and any hand-sized contact just craters the surface. Model it as applying force over a large area or as a gravitational problem. Cross-section: moon_cross_section_area.","who_when":"NASA NSSDCA, 2024-01-11"},{"key":"moon_cross_section_area","category":"object_area","label":"Moon cross-sectional area","value_si":9483000000000,"unit_si":"m^2","display":"9.48e12 m^2","status":"verified","sources":[{"url":"https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/moonfact.html","title":"NASA Moon Fact Sheet (radius)"}],"notes":"pi r^2 with r = 1,737.4 km.","who_when":"Derived"},{"key":"earth_mass","category":"object_mass","label":"Earth","value_si":5.9722e+24,"unit_si":"kg","display":"5.9722e24 kg","status":"verified","sources":[{"url":"https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html","title":"NASA NSSDCA Earth Fact Sheet (updated 15 Nov 2024)"}],"notes":"Volumetric mean radius 6,371.0 km; equatorial 6,378.137 km; mean density 5,513 kg/m^3; GM 3.9860e14 m^3/s^2. Cd(M) = 0.45 M^2 + 0.424 for 0 <= M <= 0.722. For M > 0.722, Cd(M) = 2.1 exp(-1.2(M+0.35)) - 8.9 exp(-2.2(M+0.35)) + 0.92. Sample values: M 0.3 = 0.464, M 0.9 = 0.82, M 1.0 = 0.88, peak ~1.00 at M ~1.7, M 3 = 0.95, M >= 5 = 0.92. The paper's quoted low-speed value is 0.46. This fit ignores the Reynolds-number drag crisis: a smooth sphere above Re ~3e5 can drop to ~0.1 to 0.2, and NASA Glenn gives a sphere Cd range of 0.07 to 0.5. Use for the shot, bowling ball, and any compact rounded object.","who_when":"Carter et al. (NASA NTRS 20110016614)"},{"key":"cd_cube_mach_fit","category":"drag_coefficient","label":"Cube drag coefficient vs Mach (tumbling compact bluff body)","value_si":1.09,"low_si":1.04,"high_si":1.83,"unit_si":"1","display":"~1.04-1.09 subsonic, peak ~1.83 at M 1.15, 1.67 hypersonic","status":"verified","sources":[{"url":"https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20110016614/downloads/20110016614.pdf","title":"Carter, Jandir & Kress - meteor drag (cube data to Mach 3)"}],"notes":"Cd(M) = 0.60 M^2 + 1.04 for 0 <= M <= 1.150. For M > 1.150, Cd(M) = 2.1 exp(-1.16(M+0.35)) - 6.5 exp(-2.23(M+0.35)) + 1.67. The two pieces do not join exactly at M = 1.15 (1.83 vs 1.81). The paper quotes a low-speed cube value of 1.09 and a hypersonic plateau of 1.67. Use this as the default for tumbling vehicles, pianos, tanks and buildings, with area = orientation-averaged projected area.","who_when":"Carter et al. RESEARCHER GAPS:
["Primary documents I could not read (blocked, offline or image-only PDF), so those values rely on consistent secondary sources: World Athletics C2.1 Technical Rules (shot), USBC ball spec PDF (bowling), toyota.com and Ford spec pages, Boeing 747-400 airport planning document D6-58326-1 Rev F (bot-blocked), navy.mil CVN fact file (403), toureiffel.paris key figures and the SETE press release (403; seen only via search index), Encyclopedia Titanica (403), JOM Felkins 1998 (403), ASM MatWeb (503), Georgia DOE curb-weight table (now 404).","School bus: no manufacturer-published curb weight found. The 21,000 lb figure is from a Georgia DOE table now offline, and the 18,000-25,000 lb range is from secondary guides.","Steinway Model D: the official Steinway UK page contradicts itself (990 lb = 449 kg, labelled 480 kg; header says 500 kg). Case height not verified.","Statue of Liberty: copper (62,000 / 176,000 / 200,000 lb) and framework (250,000 / 264,000 / 440,000 lb) weights genuinely conflict across NPS documents. No authoritative reconciliation found.","M1A2 SEPv3: official Army handbook not opened. The 'combat loaded 76-78 tons' quote does not specify the ton type.","Empire State Building: the owner's '365,000 tons' has no stated method, ton type, or scope (foundations/contents). Projected area not quantified (tower width above setbacks not found).","Mount Everest: no peer-reviewed or agency mass estimate found. The mass here is my own cone calculation, the base-camp elevations defining the base plane were not verified, and the popular 1.6e14 kg figure is untraceable.","Cumulus cloud: only the USGS illustrative value (0.5 g/m^3, 1 km^3). No sourced range for liquid water content or cloud size.","Material strengths not quantified: baseball leather cover, bowling-ball coverstock/core, human soft tissue, blue whale skin/blubber, Al-Li 2195 external tank (absolute yield), RHA yield (only hardness found), Eiffel Tower's own puddled iron yield, SD70ACe underframe steel and coupler strength, MT-07 frame material, F-150 body alloy grade, specific 747/A380 skin alloys and thicknesses (GLARE on A380 not verified), car body panel thickness.","Geometry not verified: F-150 width, semi overall length and height (state-regulated), Space Shuttle SRB diameter and orbiter frontal area, Nimitz keel-to-flight-deck height, blue whale girth (spheroid assumption), Eiffel Tower height (324 vs 330 m) and base size, 747-400 wing and fuselage areas. Tumbling projected areas for the 747, Eiffel Tower and ESB not quantified.","Global average adult mass of 62 kg appears only in a news write-up of Walpole et al. 2012. The abstract I could read gives only the 287 Mt total.","Typical-motorcycle choice (Yamaha MT-07) is a definitional pick, not a statistical average. No registration-weighted average motorcycle mass found.","Blue whale maxima beyond the 190 t weighed record are disputed models (Motani & Pyenson 2024 ~252-273 t for 33 m vs Paul & Larramendi 2025).","Drag: no sourced Cd for tumbling airliners, launch stacks, lattice towers, or whale bodies. The bluff-body bracket of 1.0-1.3 is an engineering estimate."]

Reasoning: dry asphalt's coarse macrotexture lets claw tips interlock with aggregate, giving roughly rubber-like grip. Wet surfaces would be lower. A foot on a large slab gets the full sqrt(A2/A1) = 2. Value: 1.7 x 24.13 MPa = 41 MPa. Low: 0.85 x 17.24 MPa (no confinement benefit). High: 1.7 x 27.58 MPa. This is a code nominal limit; actual crushing under a confined punch can be higher. In practice the slab punches through or cracks in flexure well before the surface crushes (see next entries). The secondary source cites the ACI 318 bearing clause; I could not open the code text.","who_when":"ACI 318 bearing provisions"},{"key":"ground_concrete_punching_shear_stress_aci","category":"ground_concrete_slab","label":"Concrete two-way (punching) shear stress capacity, ACI 318","status":"verified","value_si":1620000,"unit_si":"Pa","low_si":1370000,"high_si":1730000,"display":"v_c = 4 lambda sqrt(f'c) psi = 0.33 lambda sqrt(f'c) MPa (smallest of three ACI expressions); critical perimeter b0 at d/2 from the loaded area","sources":[{"title":"StructurePoint: GammaF in two-way slab punching shear (ACI 318-14)","url":"https://structurepoint.org/publication/pdf/The%20Role%20of%20GammaF%20in%20Two-way%20Slab%20Punching%20Shear%20Calculations%20in%20ACI%20318.pdf"}],"notes":"v_c = min(4, 2 + 4/beta, alpha_s*d/b0 + 2) x lambda*sqrt(f'c) psi. Values computed for f'c = 17.24-27.58 MPa (central 24.13 MPa). This is for structural two-way slabs. Plain slabs-on-ground are designed differently (ACI 360, not checked), and subgrade support inside the perimeter adds capacity.","who_when":"ACI 318-14 two-way shear provisions"},{"key":"ground_concrete_slab_on_grade_punch_through_estimate","category":"ground_concrete_slab","label":"Slab-on-grade: average foot pressure to punch through (0.1 m^2 foot)","status":"estimate","value_si":2500000,"unit_si":"Pa","low_si":2300000,"high_si":8000000,"display":"~2.5 MPa (100 mm residential slab) to ~8 MPa (200 mm, 34 MPa slab)","sources":[{"title":"Formula basis: ACI 318 two-way shear (StructurePoint)","url":"https://structurepoint.org/publication/pdf/The%20Role%20of%20GammaF%20in%20Two-way%20Slab%20Punching%20Shear%20Calculations%20in%20ACI%20318.pdf"}],"notes":"My calculation: V = 0.33*sqrt(f'c)*b0*d, with b0 = 4(B + d), B = 0.316 m and d taken as the slab thickness. Cases: 100 mm at 17-21 MPa gives V ~ 0.23-0.25 MN (about 2.3-2.5 MPa under the foot). 150 mm at 27.6 MPa gives ~0.48 MN. 200 mm at 34.5 MPa gives ~0.80 MN. Caveats: this ignores subgrade reaction (which raises capacity), plain-concrete and reinforcement effects, and flexural cracking (which may come first). After cracking the slab acts as broken plates on the subgrade.","who_when":"Estimate, 2026-10"},{"key":"ground_concrete_claw_traction_coefficient","category":"ground_concrete_slab","label":"Concrete: friction coefficient, keratin scales/claws","status":"estimate","value_si":0.6,"unit_si":"1","low_si":0.4,"high_si":0.8,"display":"~0.6 (0.4 smooth/troweled to 0.8 broom-finished)","sources":[{"title":"Context: IBC Table 1806.2 friction coefficients (concrete footing on soil/rock)","url":"https://gocodebook.com/library/us/ca/ca-building-code/chapter-18-soils-and-foundations/section-1806-presumptive-load-bearing-values-of-soils"}],"notes":"My estimate; no measured data found. Keratin cannot penetrate concrete, so this is surface friction plus claw-tip catching on texture. Steel-troweled slabs are at the low end, broom-finished at the high end.","who_when":"Estimate, 2026-10"},{"key":"ground_granite_ucs","category":"ground_granite_bedrock","label":"Intact granite: uniaxial compressive strength (UCS)","status":"verified","value_si":200000000,"unit_si":"Pa","low_si":100000000,"high_si":300000000,"display":"~100-250+ MPa; fresh granite is an ISRM 'extremely strong' (>250 MPa) example","sources":[{"title":"Hoek, Practical Rock Engineering, Ch. 11, Table 2 (field estimates of UCS)","url":"https://www.rocscience.com/assets/resources/learning/hoek/Practical-Rock-Engineering-Chapter-11-Rock-Mass-Properties.pdf"},{"title":"BGS OR/15/065 Appendix 2 (rock strength classes)","url":"https://earthwise.bgs.ac.uk/index.php/OR/15/065_Appendix_2_-_Strength,_consistency_and_density_classification_terms_and_descriptions"}],"notes":"Hoek's Table 2 classes are R5 Very strong 100-250 MPa (examples include granodiorite and gneiss) and R6 Extremely strong >250 MPa (examples include fresh granite and quartzite). Hoek gives m_i = 32 +/- 3 for granite. Weathered granite is far weaker. The 200 MPa central value and the 300 MPa high end are my choices; 300 MPa is not a hard ceiling.","who_when":"Hoek (Practical Rock Engineering); Brown 1981 grades"},{"key":"ground_granite_bearing_confinement_factor","category":"ground_granite_bedrock","label":"Rock under a small punch: ultimate bearing / UCS (confinement factor)","status":"estimate","value_si":8.5,"unit_si":"1","low_si":1,"high_si":13.8,"display":"q_ult ~ (N_phi + 1) x UCS (strip) x 1.25 (square); N_phi = tan^2(45 + phi/2) -> ~8.5-14 for intact rock; lower bound ~1 x UCS","sources":[{"title":"USACE EM 1110-1-2908 Rock Foundations (1994), Eqs 6-2, 6-4, 6-5, 6-7 and Table 6-1","url":"https://www.cedengineering.com/userfiles/Rock%20Foundations-R1.pdf"}],"notes":"Derivation from the EM 1110-1-2908 equations: local-shear q_ult = c*N_c (+ 0.5*gamma*B*N_gamma), with N_c = 2*N_phi^0.5*(N_phi + 1). For intact rock the lower-bound cohesion is c = q_u/(2*tan(45 + phi/2)) (Eq 6-7a, s = 1). Together these give q_ult ~ q_u*(N_phi + 1) for a strip, times 1.25 for a square (Sowers). For an assumed intact friction angle phi = 45-55 deg, N_phi = 5.8-10.1, so the factor is 6.8-11.1 (strip) or 8.5-13.8 (square). The phi range is my assumption, not sourced. Poorly confined, jointed rock columns fail near the unconfined strength (Eq 6-5: 2c*tan(45 + phi/2) = q_u), so the factor drops toward 1. Secondary sources attribute q_ult = q_u(N_phi + 1) to Goodman (1989); I did not open Goodman.","who_when":"Estimate built on USACE EM 1110-1-2908 (30 Nov 1994)"},{"key":"ground_granite_ultimate_bearing_small_punch","category":"ground_granite_bedrock","label":"Intact granite: ultimate bearing under a 0.1 m^2 foot","status":"estimate","value_si":1700000000,"unit_si":"Pa","low_si":100000000,"high_si":4100000000,"display":"~1.7 GPa (0.1-4 GPa)","sources":[{"title":"USACE EM 1110-1-2908","url":"https://www.cedengineering.com/userfiles/Rock%20Foundations-R1.pdf"},{"title":"Hoek Ch. 11","url":"https://www.rocscience.com/assets/resources/learning/hoek/Practical-Rock-Engineering-Chapter-11-Rock-Mass-Properties.pdf"}],"notes":"UCS x confinement factor: 200 MPa x 8.5 = 1.7 GPa. Low: jointed or weathered rock at about its UCS (100 MPa x 1). High: 300 MPa x 13.8. Real outcrops are jointed, and the joints often govern.","who_when":"Estimate, 2026-10"},{"key":"ground_granite_presumptive_allowable","category":"ground_granite_bedrock","label":"Crystalline bedrock (granite): presumptive ALLOWABLE bearing","status":"verified","value_si":7660800,"unit_si":"Pa","low_si":574560,"high_si":7660800,"display":"NAVFAC/USACE massive crystalline rock, hard sound: 160 ksf (7.66 MPa); IBC Class 1 crystalline bedrock 12,000 psf (575 kPa)","sources":[{"title":"USACE EM 1110-1-1905 Table 4-8","url":"https://www.tugraz.at/fileadmin/user_upload/Institute/IAG/Files/18_Bearing_Capacity_of_Soils-USACE.pdf"},{"title":"IBC/CBC Table 1806.2","url":"https://gocodebook.com/library/us/ca/ca-building-code/chapter-18-soils-and-foundations/section-1806-presumptive-load-bearing-values-of-soils"}],"notes":"ALLOWABLE values. The 2.49e32 J PREM value is quoted by Wikipedia, which cites only the PREM model (Dziewonski & Anderson 1981), not the calculation. I did not reproduce it.","who_when":"Wikipedia (derived from PREM 1981)"},{"key":"energy_xkcd_relativistic_baseball","category":"energy_reference","label":"xkcd What If #1 'Relativistic Baseball' (0.9c pitch): kinetic energy","status":"estimate","value_si":16865000000000000,"unit_si":"J","low_si":16520000000000000,"high_si":17330000000000000,"display":"~1.7 x 10^16 J (~4.0 Mt TNT); the article itself states no energy figure","sources":[{"title":"xkcd What If? #1 Relativistic Baseball","url":"https://what-if.xkcd.com/1/"},{"title":"Wikipedia: Baseball (ball) (5-5.25 oz per MLB rules)","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball_(ball)"}],"notes":"The web article gives NO energy number. It describes plasma, fusion and everything within about a mile of the park being levelled. My calculation: KE = (gamma - 1)mc^2 with gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - 0.81) = 2.294 and m = 0.145 kg gives 1.687e16 J (about 4.03 Mt). The range covers the 142-149 g rule limits.","who_when":"Munroe 2012 (scenario); energy derived 2026-10"},{"key":"seismic_gutenberg_richter_energy_magnitude","category":"seismic","label":"Gutenberg-Richter energy-magnitude relation","status":"verified","unit_si":"J","display":"log10 E_s = 1.5 M + 4.8 (E_s in J)  ==  log10 E_s = 1.5 M_s + 11.8 (E_s in erg)","sources":[{"title":"Collins, Melosh & Marcus (2005) Meteoritics & Planetary Science 40(6):817-840, Eq. 40 ('classic Gutenberg-Richter magnitude energy relation', citing Melosh 1989 p. 67)","url":"https://impact.ese.ic.ac.uk/static/effects.pdf"}],"notes":"Original: Gutenberg & Richter (1956), Annali di Geofisica 9:1-15, which I did not open. The joule form is confirmed by consistency with Collins Eq. 40: inserting E_s = 1e-4 x E into log E_s = 1.5M + 4.8 gives M = 0.667 log10 E - 5.87, exactly their equation. Each magnitude unit is about 31.6x in energy. USGS separately gives log E = 5.24 + 1.44 Mw without stating units; do not mix the two.","who_when":"Gutenberg & Richter 1956 (via Collins et al. 2005)"},{"key":"seismic_collins_impact_magnitude","category":"seismic","label":"Impact seismic magnitude (Earth Impact Effects Program)","status":"verified","unit_si":"1","display":"M = 0.67 log10 E - 5.87 (E = impactor kinetic energy in J; includes seismic efficiency 1e-4)","sources":[{"title":"Collins et al. 2005, Eq. 40","url":"https://impact.ese.ic.ac.uk/static/effects.pdf"}],"notes":"Collins also gives distance-dependent effective magnitudes (Eq. 41a-c), e.g. M_eff = M - 0.0238 r_km for r < 60 km.","who_when":"Collins, Melosh & Marcus 2005"},{"key":"seismic_efficiency_impact","category":"seismic","label":"Seismic efficiency of impacts (fraction of KE radiated as seismic waves)","status":"verified","value_si":0.0001,"unit_si":"1","low_si":0.00001,"high_si":0.001,"display":"1 x 10^-4 (literature range 10^-5 to 10^-3)","sources":[{"title":"Collins et al. 2005 (citing Schultz & Gault 1975)","url":"https://impact.ese.ic.ac.uk/static/effects.pdf"}],"notes":"Described there as 'the most commonly accepted figure based on experimental data'. Applying it to stomps and punches is an extrapolation.","who_when":"Collins et al. 2005; Schultz & Gault 1975"},{"key":"blast_kinney_graham_peak_overpressure","category":"blast","label":"Kinney & Graham (1985) peak overpressure vs scaled distance","status":"verified","unit_si":"1","display":"dP/P_a = 808[1 + (Z/4.5)^2] / { sqrt(1 + (Z/0.048)^2) * sqrt(1 + (Z/0.32)^2) * sqrt(1 + (Z/1.35)^2) },  Z = f_d R / W^(1/3)  [R in m, W in kg TNT, Z in m/kg^(1/3)]","sources":[{"title":"McFadden, Brown, Vida & Spurny (2021) Fireball characteristics derivable from acoustic data, arXiv:2102.06574, Eqs 11-13","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.06574"},{"title":"McFadden, Brown & Vida (2024) arXiv:2408.04078, Eqs 4-5","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.04078"},{"title":"Kinney & Graham (1985) Explosive Shocks in Air, 2nd ed., Springer (original; not opened)","url":"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-86682-1"}],"notes":"Overpressure is relative to ambient pressure P_a, so absolute dP = P_a x (ratio). The fit is for a spherical free-air chemical (TNT) explosion. Sanity checks (my calculation): Z = 1 gives a ratio of about 9.9 (~1 MPa); Z = 10 gives about 0.098 (~10 kPa). The McFadden papers scale to a 1 kt reference yield, but the classic constants (0.048, 0.32, 1.35, 4.5) belong with Z in m/kg^(1/3) and W in kg TNT. Check the convention before use. Not verified: K&G's stated Z validity limits and the usual surface-burst reflection factor (~1.8-2 x W).","who_when":"Kinney & Graham 1985"},{"key":"blast_kinney_graham_transmission_factor","category":"blast","label":"K&G atmospheric transmission (ambient scaling) factor f_d","status":"verified","unit_si":"1","display":"f_d = (P/P0)^(1/3) (T0/T)^(1/3)  (path-averaged form: f_d = [1/(h2 - h1)] * Integral[(P/P0)^(1/3) (T0/T)^(1/3) dh]); P0 = 101325 Pa, T0 = 288 K","sources":[{"title":"McFadden et al. 2021, Eq. 13","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.06574"}],"notes":"Use with Z = f_d R / W^(1/3). In thin air f_d < 1, so the same charge gives a smaller scaled distance but the overpressure is multiplied by the lower ambient P_a.","who_when":"Kinney & Graham 1985 via McFadden 2021"},{"key":"blast_collins_surface_burst_overpressure","category":"blast","label":"Collins et al. surface-burst peak overpressure fit (1 kt scaled)","status":"verified","unit_si":"Pa","display":"p = (p_x r_x / (4 r1)) * (1 + 3 (r_x/r1)^1.3), p_x = 75,000 Pa, r_x = 290 m, r1 = r / E_kt^(1/3)","sources":[{"title":"Collins et al. 2005, Eqs 54 and 57 (fit to Glasstone & Dolan 1977 Fig. 3.66)","url":"https://impact.ese.ic.ac.uk/static/effects.pdf"}],"notes":"An alternative to K&G for large (nuclear- or impact-scale) surface bursts, scaled with the cube root of yield in kt. Collins notes reliability decreases with energy and that the model probably overestimates by 2-5x above ~10,000 Mt.","who_when":"Collins et al. 2005"},{"key":"blast_collins_peak_wind_speed","category":"blast","label":"Peak wind speed behind the shock (Hugoniot)","status":"verified","unit_si":"m/s","display":"u = (5p / (7 P0)) * c0 / sqrt(1 + 6p/(7 P0)), P0 = 1e5 Pa, c0 ~ 330 m/s","sources":[{"title":"Collins et al. 2005, Eq. 59 (from Glasstone & Dolan 1977 p. 97)","url":"https://impact.ese.ic.ac.uk/static/effects.pdf"}],"notes":"Glasstone & Dolan: above 40 m/s about 30% of trees are blown down; above 62 m/s up to 90%.","who_when":"Glasstone & Dolan 1977 via Collins 2005"},{"key":"blast_window_breakage","category":"blast","label":"Overpressure: typical glass window breakage","status":"verified","value_si":6900,"unit_si":"Pa","low_si":3447,"high_si":6895,"display":"0.5-1.0 psi (3.4-6.9 kPa): windows usually shatter","sources":[{"title":"Glasstone & Dolan (1977) The Effects of Nuclear Weapons, Table 5.145","url":"https://www.fourmilab.ch/etexts/www/effects/eonw_5.pdf"},{"title":"Collins et al. 2005, Table 4 (6,900 Pa: glass windows shatter)","url":"https://impact.ese.ic.ac.uk/static/effects.pdf"}],"notes":"Side-on peak overpressure for large and small panes (shattering, occasional frame failure). Occasional breakage happens at lower pressures, but I did not verify a figure. Elsewhere, Glasstone puts light damage to most structures at about 1 psi.","who_when":"Glasstone & Dolan 1977"},{"key":"blast_eardrum_rupture_threshold","category":"blast","label":"Overpressure: eardrum rupture threshold","status":"verified","value_si":34474,"unit_si":"Pa","display":"5 psi (34.5 kPa)","sources":[{"title":"Glasstone & Dolan 1977, Table 12.38","url":"https://www.fourmilab.ch/etexts/www/effects/eonw_12.pdf"},{"title":"NASA Dryden Fact Sheet FS-2003-11-016: Sonic Booms (eardrum damage at 720 psf)","url":"https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/120274main_fs-016-dfrc.pdf"}],"notes":"Effective peak overpressure for fast-rising, long-duration (>=0.1 s) pulses. Ruptures have been recorded from 5 up to 40-50 psi. Thresholds rise for the millisecond pulses of small charges.","who_when":"Glasstone & Dolan 1977"},{"key":"blast_eardrum_rupture_50pct","category":"blast","label":"Overpressure: 50% eardrum rupture","status":"verified","value_si":120700,"unit_si":"Pa","low_si":103421,"high_si":241316,"display":"15-20 psi (103-138 kPa) for people over 20; 30-35 psi (207-241 kPa) for people under 20","sources":[{"title":"Glasstone & Dolan 1977, Table 12.38","url":"https://www.fourmilab.ch/etexts/www/effects/eonw_12.pdf"}],"notes":"The 120.7 kPa value_si is my midpoint of the adult band (17.5 psi), not a tabulated number. Fast-rising, long-duration pulse.","who_when":"Glasstone & Dolan 1977"},{"key":"blast_lethality_threshold","category":"blast","label":"Overpressure: lethality (direct blast) threshold / 50% / ~100%","status":"verified","value_si":427475,"unit_si":"Pa","low_si":275790,"high_si":634318,"display":"threshold 40 (30-50) psi = 276 kPa; 50% 62 (50-75) psi = 427 kPa; ~100% 92 (75-115) psi = 634 kPa","sources":[{"title":"Glasstone & Dolan 1977, Table 12.38","url":"https://www.fourmilab.ch/etexts/www/effects/eonw_12.pdf"}],"notes":"value_si is the 50% level; low_si is the threshold and high_si the ~100% level. Primary blast only. In practice, debris and being thrown kill at far lower pressures.","who_when":"Glasstone & Dolan 1977"},{"key":"blast_residential_collapse","category":"blast","label":"Overpressure: wood-frame house almost complete collapse","status":"verified","value_si":26800,"unit_si":"Pa","low_si":22900,"high_si":26800,"display":"26.8 kPa (~3.9 psi) near-complete collapse; 22.9 kPa interior partitions blown down and roof severely damaged","sources":[{"title":"Collins et al. 2005, Table 4 (data from Glasstone & Dolan 1977)","url":"https://impact.ese.ic.ac.uk/static/effects.pdf"}],"notes":"Derived from a 1 kt (nuclear, long-duration) blast. Rare minor damage occurs at 2-5 psf (96-239 Pa). Structures in good condition were undamaged up to 11 psf (527 Pa). People have experienced 20-144 psf (0.96-6.9 kPa) without injury.","who_when":"NASA DFRC 2003"},{"key":"crater_collins_transient_diameter","category":"cratering","label":"Transient crater diameter (Collins, Melosh & Marcus 2005)","status":"verified","unit_si":"m","display":"D_tc = 1.161 (rho_i/rho_t)^(1/3) L^0.78 v_i^0.44 g^-0.22 (sin theta)^(1/3)","sources":[{"title":"Collins et al. 2005, Eq. 21","url":"https://impact.ese.ic.ac.uk/static/effects.pdf"}],"notes":"SI units: D_tc in m, measured at the pre-impact surface. rho_i and rho_t are impactor and target densities (kg/m^3); L is impactor diameter at the surface (m); v_i is impact speed at the surface (m/s); g = 9.81 m/s^2; theta is the impact angle from horizontal. Use 1.365 in place of 1.161 for water targets. The constants are uncertain within 0.8-1.5. The program uses target densities of 2500 (sedimentary) and 2750 (crystalline) kg/m^3. Valid in the GRAVITY regime for solid-rock targets, i.e. terrestrial impacts larger than a few hundred metres. It does not apply to small, strength-dominated craters, so it should not be used for a punch or stomp crater without a strength-regime scaling. Transient depth d_tc = D_tc / (2*sqrt(2)) (Eq. 25).","who_when":"Collins, Melosh & Marcus 2005"},{"key":"crater_collins_simple_final_diameter","category":"cratering","label":"Simple crater final rim-to-rim diameter","status":"verified","unit_si":"m","display":"D_fr ~ 1.25 D_tc  (simple craters: D_tc <= 2.56 km)","sources":[{"title":"Collins et al. 2005, Eq. 22","url":"https://impact.ese.ic.ac.uk/static/effects.pdf"}],"notes":"Complex craters (D_tc > 2.56 km): D_fr = 1.17 D_tc^1.13 / D_c^0.13 (both in km), with D_c = 3.2 km (Eq. 27, McKinnon & Schenk 1985 form). Breccia lens volume V_br ~ 0.032 D_fr^3.","who_when":"Collins et al. 2005"},{"key":"aero_stagnation_temperature_formula","category":"aerothermal","label":"Stagnation (total) temperature, calorically perfect gas","status":"verified","unit_si":"K","display":"T0 = T [1 + (gamma - 1)/2 * M^2], gamma = 1.4","sources":[{"title":"NASA Glenn BGH: Stagnation Temperature - Real Gas Effects","url":"https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/BGH/stagtmp.html"}],"notes":"Isentropic total-temperature relation. Total temperature does not change across a shock, so it equals the stagnation-point temperature.","who_when":"NASA GRC"},{"key":"aero_real_gas_validity_caution","category":"aerothermal","label":"Validity limit of the perfect-gas stagnation formula","status":"verified","unit_si":"1","display":"Diverges from about Mach 3 (vibrational excitation); at higher Mach O2/N2 dissociate and then ionize, so T0 is greatly over-predicted at hypersonic speeds","sources":[{"title":"NASA Glenn BGH: Stagnation Temperature - Real Gas Effects","url":"https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/BGH/stagtmp.html"},{"title":"NASA Glenn BGH: Real gas effects","url":"https://www.grc.nasa.gov/www/BGH/realgas.html"},{"title":"CAIB Report Vol. I (2003), section 3.6","url":"http://s3.amazonaws.com/akamai.netstorage/anon.nasa-global/CAIB/CAIB_lowres_full.pdf"}],"notes":"NASA: below Mach 3 the perfect and imperfect values agree; 'beginning around Mach 3, real gas effects become increasingly important'. NASA gives a variable-gamma correction (theta = 5500 deg R, NACA Report 1135). Illustration (my calculation): at Mach 25 with T = 216.65 K, the perfect-gas formula gives about 27,300 K, whereas CAIB says the dissociated air at the Shuttle leading edge reaches about 10,000 deg F (~5,800 K). Dissociation onset temperatures (often quoted as roughly 2,000-2,500 K for O2 and 4,000 K for N2 at 1 atm) were NOT verified here. Above about Mach 5-6 the engine should use a real-gas model or cap temperatures.","who_when":"NASA GRC; CAIB 2003"},{"key":"aero_shuttle_peak_surface_temperature","category":"aerothermal","label":"Space Shuttle reentry: nose cap / wing leading edge temperature","status":"verified","value_si":1922,"unit_si":"K","low_si":1811,"high_si":1922,"display":"2,800-3,000 deg F (1,811-1,922 K); other wing/fuselage areas up to 2,300 deg F (1,533 K)","sources":[{"title":"Columbia Accident Investigation Board Report, Vol. I (2003), Ch. 1 and section 3.6","url":"http://s3.amazonaws.com/akamai.netstorage/anon.nasa-global/CAIB/CAIB_lowres_full.pdf"}],"notes":"CAIB: 'The nose and leading edges of the wings are exposed to superheated air temperatures of 2,800 to 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit, depending upon re-entry profile.' Wing leading edge temperatures normally reached nearly 3,000 deg F. Conversion: K = (F - 32) x 5/9 + 273.15.","who_when":"CAIB 2003"},{"key":"aero_shuttle_shock_layer_air_temperature","category":"aerothermal","label":"Space Shuttle reentry: air temperature near the leading edge (shock layer)","status":"verified","value_si":5811,"unit_si":"K","display":"~10,000 deg F (~5,800 K), dissociated air","sources":[{"title":"CAIB Report Vol. I, section 3.6","url":"http://s3.amazonaws.com/akamai.netstorage/anon.nasa-global/CAIB/CAIB_lowres_full.pdf"}],"notes":"CAIB: the flow behind the shocks is hot enough that air molecules are dissociated; 'the air immediately around the leading edge surface can reach 10,000 degrees Fahrenheit', while the boundary layer keeps the surface near 3,000 deg F. This is a good real-world cap for comparison with the perfect-gas formula.","who_when":"CAIB 2003"}]

["The web search budget ran out partway through. After that I could only open pages whose URLs I already had, so some items below might be findable with more searching.","Sea ice compressive strength: the authoritative review (Timco & Weeks 2010, Cold Regions Sci. Tech.) is paywalled and its abstract could not be retrieved, so no value is given. The ice shear strength value and the floating-ice-sheet bearing formula (Gold's formula) were also not verified.","Friction and traction coefficients for keratin scales and claws on every surface: I found no measured data. All values are reasoned estimates (soil friction angle or s_u times area for soils, surface-texture judgment for hard surfaces).","Asphalt pavement: I found no published ultimate static punch capacity or shear strength for asphalt concrete. Only the aviation tyre-pressure categories (allowable, repeated load) are verified; the 1-5 MPa ultimate is an order-of-magnitude estimate.","Reinforced-concrete building severe-damage overpressure: Glasstone & Dolan give it only in the Fig. 5.140 nomograph, which I could not extract. No numeric value is given.","Kinney & Graham (1985) book not opened. The stated validity range of Z and the standard surface-burst reflection multiplier (~1.8-2 x W) are unverified. The equation and transmission factor are verified through McFadden et al. 2021 (peer-reviewed).","Gutenberg & Richter (1956) original not opened. The joule form log10 E = 1.5M + 4.8 is verified only by its exact consistency with Collins et al. 2005 Eq. 40. USGS's page gives a different relation (log E = 5.24 + 1.44 Mw) without units.","MOAB yield: no primary source found (GlobalSecurity paywalled; Wikipedia's infobox has no citation). The kind of 'ton' is ambiguous.","Hiroshima yield: the LANL primary report (Malik 1985, LA-8819) was not opened; the value is via Wikipedia. Castle Bravo: the official DOE/NV-209 test list could not be retrieved (404); the value is via Nuclear Weapon Archive.","Krakatoa 1883: only the single 'about 200 Mt' figure was found, via Wikipedia citing a Bureau of Meteorology page that no longer has the content. No sourced range.","Chicxulub: only one peer-reviewed range was checked (1.3e24-5.8e25 J). Other commonly quoted values were not verified, so no single value is given.","Earth gravitational binding energy: the PREM-based 2.49e32 J is quoted from Wikipedia, which cites only the density model. I did not reproduce the integral. The uniform-density 2.24e32 J was computed.","xkcd What If #1: the web article gives no energy figure. The ~1.7e16 J (~4 Mt) is my own relativistic KE calculation. The book version was not checked.","Dissociation onset temperatures for O2/N2 (often quoted ~2,000-2,500 K and ~4,000 K) and a precise 'Mach 5-6' threshold were not verified. NASA GRC gives only the qualitative onset of real-gas effects from about Mach 3.","Intact granite friction angle (45-55 deg) used for the rock bearing confinement factor is my assumption. The Goodman (1989) q_ult = q_u(N_phi + 1) attribution and the Carter & Kulhawy Hoek-Brown bearing formula were not verified from primary sources.","Concrete slab-on-grade: an industrial-floor f'c above 4,000 psi and the ACI 360 slab-on-ground punching method were not verified. The punch-through estimate uses the ACI 318 structural-slab formula, ignores subgrade support, and is labelled as an estimate.","A36 steel properties and the indentation constraint factor (~3) come from secondary sources (Wikipedia citing the AISC Manual and Fischer-Cripps 2007). ASTM and AISC pages were blocked. The AISC 0.6 Fy shear convention was not verified.","IUGG mean Earth radius R1 = 6371.0088 km was not verified; the NASA 6371.000 km volumetric mean radius was used.","ISA sea-level density, temperature, lapse rate and gas constant come from the Wikipedia summary of ICAO Doc 7488. The ICAO document itself was not opened, but the values are mutually consistent with the NIST pressure and ideal-gas law.","Clay strength bands: the 'ASTM D-2488' kPa bands come from a software library's documentation (secondary). BS 5930 bands are confirmed via BGS and ISO 14688-2 via Geocentrix (secondary)."]
